preamble: Before committing or shipping non-trivial code, check it against these recurring root-cause classes (distilled from cross-project review history). Each is a question to ask of the diff, not a style rule. When a fix lands in one of these classes, tag the commit `Class: <slug>` (the review-fix commit convention).

classes.question: Multiple processes/sessions read+write the same dir or file (a sandbox HOME, a SQLite db, LEARNINGS subfiles). Is concurrent access coordinated (flock / atomic temp-then-rename / append), and does a partial or stale read fail loudly instead of silently?

Before changing OR REMOVING a shared artifact — a marker, a config key, an on-disk schema, a parsed contract, a CLI command — enumerate EVERY producer and consumer, not just the one in front of you. Search past this repo's boundary: skills, agent briefs, runbooks and hook registrations call your code and never appear in your diff. Docs that restate a default you are changing count too.

Sentinel/marker/status files and flags: get the full lifecycle right — creation, detection, clearing, and the stale-marker race. What happens if the marker is left over from a prior run, or never written?
Never assume an agent/LLM returns well-formed output. Handle empty, whitespace-only, malformed, truncated, and wrong-schema responses explicitly at the boundary.

Mismatched units (seconds vs ms, UTC vs local time) and unanchored matches (relative vs absolute paths, un-anchored regex or ID matching). Make units explicit and convert at the boundary; anchor paths and patterns.

A cached or derived artifact (an install, a build output, a sidecar): does its key include the version of the code that PRODUCED it, not just its input's identity? A key that omits the producer keeps serving the old answer after the code changes, and stale looks exactly like fresh.

Does each touched test actually fail when the behaviour it names breaks? Watch for assertions that hold either way, and fixed sleeps standing in for a condition — those pass in isolation and flake under load. A test that passes for the wrong reason masks the regression it was meant to catch.

Does every new detector, guard, or validation check in this change have a proven known positive (you watched it fire on input it must catch) and a known negative (it stayed quiet on clean input)? A clean pass from an unproven check is instrument failure, not evidence — and so is an alarm from one.
